prompt: Why can't Br2 in acetic acid be used to α-brominate carboxylic acids?

choices.text: Carboxylic acids don't enolize to a sufficient extent
Carboxylic acids have no α hydrogens
choices.why: Many do; heptanoic acid, for example, is α-brominated to 2-bromoheptanoic acid by the HVZ reaction. The problem is how little acids enolize.

choices.text: Br2 adds to the C=O bond of the acid instead
choices.why: The limitation the section gives is that acids, esters, and amides don't enolize enough.

choices.text: Carboxylic acids are brominated on the oxygen of the –OH group
choices.why: Bromination in acetic acid fails because the acid barely enolizes, not because it reacts somewhere else.

explanation: α Bromination by Br2 in acetic acid is limited to aldehydes and ketones because acids, esters, and amides don't enolize to a sufficient extent. Carboxylic acids are α-brominated instead by the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii (HVZ) reaction.

prompt: Which reagents carry out the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii (HVZ) reaction?

choices.text: Br2 and PBr3, followed by water

choices.why: That works for aldehydes and ketones, not for carboxylic acids, which don't enolize enough.
PBr3 converts the acid to an acid bromide, but Br2 is needed to put a bromine on the α carbon.
HBr catalyzes enolization of the acid bromide, but without PBr3 and Br2 there is no acid bromide and no bromine source.

explanation: Carboxylic acids are α-brominated by a mixture of Br2 and PBr3 in the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii reaction. Adding water at the end hydrolyzes the α-bromo acid bromide to the α-bromo carboxylic acid.

prompt: In the HVZ reaction, which enol actually reacts with Br2?

choices.text: The enol of an acid bromide formed with PBr3
The enol of the carboxylic acid itself
choices.why: The HVZ reaction involves α substitution of an acid bromide enol rather than a carboxylic acid enol.

choices.text: An enolate ion made with a strong base
choices.why: The HVZ reaction is acid-catalyzed: HBr catalyzes enolization of the acid bromide.

choices.text: The enol of the α-bromo carboxylic acid product
choices.why: The product forms only after bromination and hydrolysis. The enol that reacts with Br2 is the acid bromide's.

explanation: The carboxylic acid first reacts with PBr3 to form an acid bromide plus HBr. The HBr catalyzes enolization of the acid bromide, and this enol reacts with Br2 in an α-substitution reaction to give an α-bromo acid bromide. Water then hydrolyzes it by nucleophilic acyl substitution.

prompt: What is the product when heptanoic acid, CH3(CH2)5CO2H, is treated with Br2 and PBr3, followed by water?

choices.why: The HVZ reaction brominates the α carbon, carbon 2, not the end of the chain.
The acid bromide is an intermediate. It is α-brominated, and water then turns it back into a carboxylic acid.
That α-bromo acid bromide is the intermediate before water is added. Water hydrolyzes it to the acid.

explanation: The HVZ reaction converts heptanoic acid into 2-bromoheptanoic acid (90% yield). The α-bromo acid bromide intermediate is hydrolyzed by water in the last step.

prompt: If methanol rather than water is added at the end of an HVZ reaction of 3-methylpentanoic acid, CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CO2H, what is the product?

choices.why: That is the product when water is added at the end. Methanol gives an ester.
The bromine goes on the α carbon, carbon 2, not on carbon 3.
The α bromine is still introduced. Methanol changes only the last step, turning the acid bromide into an ester.

explanation: If methanol replaces water, the α-bromo acid bromide undergoes nucleophilic acyl substitution with methanol to give an α-bromo ester rather than an acid (Exercise 22.4.1).
